title: "Whenever dharma declines, I come" (4.1–4.8)
hook: Arjuna asks how his friend could have taught the sun, and Krishna says who he really is

segments.voice: Yesterday, desire as the enemy: smoke over fire, dust over a mirror, and chapter three ended. Your line was know the enemy. Did you name a want out loud? Today, chapter four, and Krishna says who he is. Day one hundred seventy-one.

Imagine your best friend, someone you grew up with, mentions casually that he taught this same lesson to the sun, ages ago. You'd laugh. Or you'd stare. That's where chapter four begins. Krishna says: this teaching isn't new. I gave it long ago to Vivasvan, the sun. The sun passed it to Manu, the first man, and Manu to the king Ikshvaku, and down it went, king to king, until over a long time it was lost. Now I'm giving it back to you, because you're my friend. And Arjuna, very reasonably, says: wait. You were born recently. The sun was born long before. How could you have taught him?
screen: `I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN.` → `KING TO KING, THEN LOST.` → `BUT YOU WERE BORN RECENTLY.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer: many births have passed, for me and for you, Arjuna. I know them all. You don't. Then he says what he is. Though I am unborn, and my self is imperishable, and I am lord of all beings, I come into being through my own power. And then some of the most famous verses in Hindu scripture. In Sanskrit: yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata. Whenever dharma declines. Here's Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation of the two verses: "When Righteousness Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take Visible shape, and move a man with men, Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, And setting Virtue on her seat again." The last words in Sanskrit are sambhavami yuge yuge. I come into being, age after age. This is the root of the idea of the avatara, the descent: the divine coming down into the world in a form, again and again, when things go badly wrong. It's how many Hindus, especially Vaishnavas, understand Rama and Krishna, and the list of Vishnu's descents: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf Vamana you met at Onam, and more. Hindu schools read these verses in different ways. Some hear a personal God truly taking a body out of love. Others hear the one reality appearing through its own power, without ever being bound by it. But the promise sounds the same to both. It's not a promise that bad times won't come. It's a promise about what happens when they do. When the wrong grows strong, the good returns. You heard this on Janmashtami, about a baby born in a prison at midnight. Now you've heard it from his own mouth.
screen: `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `UNBORN, YET I COME INTO BEING.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES.` · `AVATARA: THE DESCENT, AGE AFTER AGE.` · then, large: `WHEN THE WRONG GROWS STRONG, HE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a return. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time when things had gone badly wrong, in your life, your family, the world, and then something good came back that you hadn't expected. A person who showed up. A kindness. A turn. Let it come back clearly. Notice that you couldn't see it coming from inside the dark part. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's promise: age after age, I come. If not, just hold the memory that good has returned before. The bell holds the time.
Whenever dharma declines. Yada yada hi dharmasya. When the right weakens and the wrong grows strong, Krishna says, I come, age after age.
Your line: he returns. Today, when the news or your day feels like the wrong is winning, remember one time the good came back. Day one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Gita 4.7–4.8, yada yada hi dharmasya, is among the most recited verses in Hinduism and is the classic statement of the avatara, the divine descent; many Vaishnava Hindus read it with the ten avatars of Vishnu in mind.

match.prompt: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.
pairs: the sun, first to receive the teaching
the descent, the divine taking form

myth: Krishna says the Gita's teaching is brand new
he says he gave it long ago to the sun, it passed king to king, and was lost.
Krishna promises bad times will never come
he promises what happens when they do: when the wrong grows strong, he comes.
Hindu schools read these verses in more than one way
some hear a personal God taking a body out of love; others, the one reality appearing through its own power.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. your friend and driver says he taught this teaching to the sun, ages ago. what do you say?
options: ask how, since he was born so recently.
fork.reveal: he asks: you were born later, the sun long before; how could you have taught him? Krishna answers with who he is, and the promise: age after age, I come.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 4.7: whenever, indeed, of dharma. the opening of the promise.

trapdoor: what you thought: God shows up to punish bad people.
what it means: whenever the right weakens and the wrong grows strong, the divine takes form, to protect the good and set dharma back on its seat.
what a scholar hears: 4.7–8 is the classic root of avatara doctrine, and 4.6 says he comes by his own maya, his own power, while remaining unborn.
